5f021dff01be.t: Acceptance Was the Answer: Big Book Page 417 Explained

a7f36aa92d27.t: The famous acceptance passage is on page 417 of the Big Book, 4th Edition. Learn what 'acceptance is the answer' really means, and what it does not.

b2d76b466ebc.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Acceptance Was the Answer: The Big Book's Page 417 Passage

23b09478a589.t: Acceptance Was the Answer: The Big Book's Page 417 Passage

f030f592a5e3.t: What the most-quoted passage in the Big Book teaches about serenity, and where acceptance ends and action begins

9b814e244533.t: The passage almost everyone is looking for sits on page 417 of <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, 4th Edition, in a personal story called <1>Acceptance Was the Answer</1>. The writer, a physician who was addicted to both alcohol and pills, opens the most-quoted paragraph in the book by telling us that 'acceptance is the answer to all my problems today' (page 417). When he is disturbed, he says, it is because he finds 'some person, place, thing, or situation' unacceptable to him, and he can find no serenity until he accepts that person, place, thing, or situation as being 'exactly the way it is supposed to be at this moment' (page 417).

5bd54f5099ac.t: If the page number looks wrong to you, you may be remembering an older printing. In the 3rd Edition this same story was titled <0>Doctor, Alcoholic, Addict</0>, and the acceptance passage fell on page 449. When the 4th Edition came out in 2001, the story was renamed and the book repaged, so the words we heard quoted as 'page 449' now live on page 417.

a1993a2240ea.t: The paragraph makes a claim big enough to argue with: 'Nothing, absolutely nothing, happens in God's world by mistake' (page 417). The doctor is not saying that everything that happens is good. He is saying that serenity begins when we stop demanding that reality be different than it is right now. He tells us he had to accept his own alcoholism before he could ever stay sober, and that 'unless I accept life completely on life's terms, I cannot be happy' (page 417). Then he turns the lens all the way around: he needed to concentrate less on what needed changing in the world and more on what needed changing in himself and his attitudes (page 417). That is the hinge of the whole passage. His hard experience distills into one line many of us keep taped to the mirror: 'When I stopped living in the problem and began living in the answer, the problem went away' (page 417).

7b6931f6b375.t: <0>Acceptance is not approval.</0> It does not mean we like what happened, that we excuse cruelty, or that we stay quietly in situations that harm us. It means we stop burning our strength in a war with facts. The basic text asks the same surrender of us about our drinking: 'We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics' (page 30). We could not recover from a condition we refused to admit we had. The same spirit shows up in the promises that follow Step Ten: 'And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol' (page 84). Ceasing to fight is not quitting on life. It is how we finally join it.

88afcdeb275d.t: Neither is acceptance a permission slip for passivity. The same book that gives us page 417 sends us out the door to make our amends (page 76) and to sweep off our side of the street (page 77), and it tells us plainly that 'Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery' (page 97). Acceptance is where action becomes possible. We accept what we cannot change so that we have the strength to change what we can, starting with ourselves.

d39422fb7006.t: A Story, Not a Set of Instructions

a30f01213615.t: It helps to know where these words live. Page 417 sits in the personal stories section of the Big Book, not in the first 164 pages that lay out the program of recovery. That does not make the passage less true. It makes it testimony. A physician is telling us what actually kept him sober, one day at a time. The stories exist to show us the principles walking around in real lives, and this one is quoted by page number in meetings all over the world. The basic text and the story agree completely: we admit what is, we turn over what we cannot manage, and we get to work on what we can.

4f4565ec105b.t: So how do we use it? The next time we are disturbed, we can try the doctor's inventory. What person, place, thing, or situation are we refusing to accept? Then comes a second question: what part of this is actually ours to change? Usually the honest answer is our own attitude and our own next action, exactly as page 417 suggests. The Big Book reminds us that what we really have is 'a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85), and acceptance is part of each day's maintenance. We do not have to accept forever, only for today. We do not have to like it, only to stop fighting it. Serenity waits on the other side of that surrender.

4c43718dc033.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: pages 30, 76, 77, 84, 85, 97, 417; story 'Acceptance Was the Answer' (Part II, They Stopped in Time). 3rd Edition: same story as 'Doctor, Alcoholic, Addict', acceptance passage on page 449.

8e13755329aa.t: What page is 'acceptance is the answer' on in the Big Book?

d0796d9e0f2b.t: It is on page 417 of the 4th Edition of Alcoholics Anonymous, in the personal story Acceptance Was the Answer. If you learned it as page 449, you are remembering the 3rd Edition, where the same story was titled Doctor, Alcoholic, Addict.

a780731f796f.t: Who wrote the story Acceptance Was the Answer?

943adfa2787b.t: A physician member of AA whose story appears in the personal stories section of the 4th Edition. Because AA members remain anonymous in print, the book does not name its story authors; he describes himself as a physician who was addicted to both alcohol and pills before he found sobriety in the fellowship.

c143b71ce304.t: Does acceptance mean I have to approve of bad things that happen?

cfa7e4f745ec.t: No. Acceptance in the Big Book sense means acknowledging reality as it actually is so we can stop fighting it and find serenity (page 417). It is not approval, resignation, or a reason to stay in harmful situations; the same passage points us toward changing ourselves and our attitudes, and the rest of the book calls us to real action, like making amends (page 76).

495bbc18e6ca.t: Is the acceptance passage part of the AA program itself?

8bcd8b0bb352.t: It comes from a member's personal story, not from the first 164 pages that describe the program of recovery. But it echoes the basic text, which asks us to fully concede our alcoholism to our innermost selves (page 30) and promises that we will cease fighting anything or anyone (page 84).

440b5e26aae7.t: Big Book Amends: Steps 8 and 9 Explained (Pages 76-84)

619a6d977d99.t: The Big Book covers amends on pages 76-84. Learn what direct amends means in Steps 8 and 9, the except-when clause, and why amends go beyond apologies.

b737225a1fae.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Making Amends in the Big Book: Steps 8 and 9

13a0184565b0.t: Making Amends in the Big Book: Steps 8 and 9

08c6a4f15fbe.t: What pages 76 to 84 ask of us, and what they promise in return

54f56bbb5ec1.t: The Big Book covers making amends on pages 76 through 84, in the chapter called Into Action. Step Eight asks us to list everyone we have harmed and become willing to make amends to them all. Step Nine asks us to make 'direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others' (page 59). The book spends barely a paragraph on Step Eight, and the reason is practical: we already made the list when we took our inventory (page 76). What remains is willingness, and the book tells us that if we do not have it yet, we keep asking until it comes.

bac7fc2817c9.t: Why do we do it at all? Page 76 opens this stretch of the book by reminding us that 'Faith without works is dead.' The spiritual experience we found in the earlier steps has to be carried into our relationships or it withers. Page 77 gives the purpose in a single sentence: 'Our real purpose is to fit ourselves to be of maximum service to God and the people about us.' We are not making amends mainly to feel better or to be forgiven. We are sweeping away the wreckage of self-will so we can be useful again.

eace2c615a59.t: What Direct Amends Actually Look Like

ddf99b10bccd.t: Direct means we go to the person, face to face wherever possible, rather than sending a vague apology from a safe distance. The book walks through real situations. We approach the person we have resented or wronged 'in a helpful and forgiving spirit' (page 77), keeping the focus on our own side of the street; his faults are not our business that day. With creditors, page 78 says we do not dodge them. We let them know we are sorry and arrange the best repayment we can. Even wrongs that could cost us our reputation or worse are on the table. Page 79 sets the standard plainly: 'We must not shrink at anything.' We ask God for strength and direction to do the right thing, whatever the personal consequences may be.

6a62f790068a.t: Step Nine carries one careful exception: we make amends except when doing so would injure the person or somebody else. Notice what the clause does not say. It does not say except when it is embarrassing, expensive, or frightening for us. The injury in question is theirs, never ours. Page 79 warns that we are not to be 'the hasty and foolish martyr' who needlessly sacrifices others to save himself. Buying our own peace of mind at another person's expense is not an amend; it is one more act of selfishness wearing Step Nine clothing. The book's examples on pages 80 and 81 involve confessions that would wound a spouse or pull innocent people into harm. In those cases we seek guidance first, talking things over with others and asking God for direction before taking any drastic step (page 80). The willingness stays total. The method stays considerate.

4cd9a0578585.t: Page 82 gives the most vivid picture in the book of why an apology is not enough: 'The alcoholic is like a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others.' A tornado cannot fix a town by saying sorry to it. Speaking of the family, page 83 is blunt: 'A remorseful mumbling that we are sorry won't fill the bill at all.' What fills the bill is repair. We pay what we owe, we tell the truth we withheld, and above all we live differently at home, day after day, so the people closest to us experience the change instead of just hearing about it. The book is also honest that some wrongs can never be fully righted. Page 83 says we do not worry about those if we can honestly say we would right them if we could. Willingness is the coin of this step.

b8eff2740bfc.t: Right in the middle of the Step Nine instructions, the book pauses to tell us what happens if we do this work thoroughly. 'If we are painstaking about this phase of our development, we will be amazed before we are half way through' (page 83). Then come the Ninth Step Promises: 'We are going to know a new freedom and a new happiness. We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' (page 83). Fear of people, self-pity, and the old feeling of uselessness begin to slip away as the amends get made. Page 84 closes the passage with the assurance generations of us have tested: 'They will always materialize if we work for them.' We do not have to finish the list this week. We simply have to start, stay willing, and keep walking toward the next name.

e7978f99768f.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition — Step 9 wording from chapter "How It Works," page 59; amends passage from chapter "Into Action," pages 76-84

07b025740142.t: What pages in the Big Book cover making amends?

2a4d8656eccb.t: Pages 76 through 84 in the chapter Into Action. Step Eight gets a single paragraph on page 76, because the list of people we harmed was already made during the Step Four inventory. The rest of the passage walks through how to make Step Nine amends, and it closes with the Ninth Step Promises on pages 83 and 84.

fbca84dbce41.t: What is the difference between making amends and apologizing?

387f979a296e.t: An apology is words; an amend is repair. The Big Book says a remorseful mumbling that we are sorry will not fill the bill (page 83). Making amends means paying the debts (page 78), telling the truth, and living differently so the people we harmed experience the change rather than just hearing about it.

fd4443b155d2.t: What does 'except when to do so would injure them or others' mean in Step 9?

d46ffd1360c4.t: It means we hold back or adjust an amend only when making it would hurt the other person or an innocent third party, not when it is merely uncomfortable for us. Page 79 warns against being the hasty and foolish martyr who sacrifices others to ease his own conscience, and page 80 counsels seeking guidance from others and from God before any drastic disclosure.

bbcf5168777d.t: Do I have to make all my amends at once?

fa43903a8509.t: No. The Big Book acknowledges that some wrongs can never be fully righted, and says we need not worry about them if we can honestly say we would right them if we could (page 83). We take the list as opportunities come, sensibly and considerately, and page 84 promises the results always materialize if we work for them.

1a6db3064ebf.t: Carrying the Message: Step 12 in the Big Book (Page 89)

815ed687e205.t: What carrying the message means in Step 12 and Chapter 7 of the Big Book, why working with other alcoholics keeps us sober, and how to actually do it.

2a738fda66bb.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Carrying the Message: Step 12 and Working With Others

e0eeec952894.t: Carrying the Message: Step 12 and Working With Others

e75702feed30.t: Why the Big Book says helping another alcoholic is the surest way to stay sober ourselves

75709bc4de19.t: Carrying the message is the heart of Step 12: <0>"Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs"</0> (page 60). The Big Book devotes an entire chapter to it, Chapter 7, Working With Others, and opens with one of the most quoted lines in the whole book: "Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (page 89). Notice what that sentence actually claims. Not that helping others is a nice extra once we feel better, but that it protects our own sobriety more reliably than anything else we can do.

986fb792b4f5.t: The same page makes it a direct instruction: "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (page 89). Then it tells us why we, of all people, are qualified: "You can help when no one else can" (page 89). Doctors, family, and friends may have tried for years to reach a drinker and failed. But one alcoholic talking honestly to another gets a hearing nobody else gets, because we have been where they are. Our drinking history, the thing we were most ashamed of, becomes the very credential that lets us reach someone still suffering.

6dfa0beeab65.t: Why Working With Others Keeps Us Sober

e95296d14ac9.t: The Big Book is blunt about our stake in this. Early in the book it says "our very lives, as ex-problem drinkers, depend upon our constant thought of others and how we may help meet their needs" (page 20). That is strong language, and it is meant to be. The alcoholic mind drifts back toward self, and self-centeredness is described on page 62 as the root of our troubles. Twelfth Step work is the practical antidote. When we sit with a newcomer, we cannot stay wrapped up in our own problems. We hear our own story out of someone else's mouth, and we remember exactly what we were saved from.

bd9e199c2f00.t: Chapter 7 also promises something beyond protection. "Life will take on new meaning" (page 89). Watching people recover, watching them turn around and help others, watching a fellowship grow up around us, the book says this is an experience we must not miss. Later in the chapter it goes further still: "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (page 97), and it adds that an occasional kindly act is not enough. This is daily material, not a merit badge we earn once.

77b477d67377.t: How We Actually Carry the Message

5264027d7324.t: The chapter is practical about method. We are told to learn what we can about the prospect first, to approach him when he is ready to listen rather than when he is very drunk, and to talk as one alcoholic to another, sharing our own drinking history before we ever mention a solution (pages 90-91). We describe ourselves as someone who has found an answer, not as someone recruiting for a cause. If he is not interested, we do not force it; the book tells us not to waste time chasing a man who cannot or will not work with us, because our job is to be useful, not to argue anyone into recovery (page 96). And carrying the message is bigger than formal Twelfth Step calls. It is sponsorship, greeting the newcomer at a meeting, sharing honestly, and letting our changed life speak. The book's closing page puts it simply: "Give freely of what you find and join us" (page 164).

2e4163e1e738.t: Step 12 begins with a condition: having had a spiritual awakening <0>as the result of these steps</0>. We carry a message we have actually received. That is why the first eleven steps matter so much; without them we have sympathy to offer, but not a solution. The awakening does not need to be dramatic. Appendix II describes most of our spiritual experiences as gradual, of the educational variety (pages 567-568). What matters is that something real has changed in us, and we give it away to keep it. Freely we received, so freely we give. That exchange, one alcoholic helping another, is the engine that has kept this fellowship alive since two men sat down together in Akron in 1935.

4738bc32f5fb.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition: Step Twelve (page 60); Chapter 7, Working With Others (pages 89-103, esp. 89, 90-91, 96, 97); Chapter 2, There Is a Solution (page 20); page 62 (selfishness as root of our troubles); page 164 (Give freely of what you find); Appendix II, Spiritual Experience (pages 567-568)

0a38b1b45559.t: What does carrying the message mean in Step 12?

6fd4bdf24efd.t: It means sharing the solution we found through the first eleven steps with alcoholics who still suffer. Step 12 reads in part that having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics (page 60). The message is not just our story; it is the program of recovery that produced our spiritual awakening.

d07f5ff2f5b5.t: What page of the Big Book says working with other alcoholics insures immunity from drinking?

3902ccfbe753.t: Page 89, the opening of Chapter 7, Working With Others. It says practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics, and adds that this kind of work succeeds when other activities fail.

daa3e6278f43.t: Do I have to sponsor someone to work Step 12?

1bdec608e2ef.t: No. Sponsorship is one powerful form of Twelfth Step work, but Chapter 7 describes many ways to be useful: making calls on prospects, welcoming newcomers, and simply being available (pages 89-90). Page 97 says helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery, and that can look like any daily act of service to another alcoholic.

93f017dac0c2.t: What if the person I try to help doesn't want to get sober?

07d0f3bc439f.t: The Big Book says not to force ourselves on anyone and calls it a waste of time to keep chasing a man who cannot or will not work with us (page 96). We plant the seed, stay friendly if we can, and move on to someone who is ready. The outcome belongs to God; our job is only to carry the message honestly.

85e91b44c61c.t: Daily Reprieve: What Big Book Page 85 Really Means

eeb39f712029.t: Big Book page 85 says we have a daily reprieve contingent on our spiritual condition. Here is what that maintenance looks like in Steps Ten and Eleven.

abbfaaf75a46.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / The Daily Reprieve on Page 85 of the Big Book

f1a72850c106.t: The Daily Reprieve on Page 85 of the Big Book

47223a3edf35.t: What maintaining our spiritual condition actually looks like, one day at a time

f51b435a972c.t: The words people remember are on page 85 of Alcoholics Anonymous, in the chapter called Into Action: 'What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85). In plain language, sobriety is not a prize we win once and keep forever. It is renewed one day at a time, and it holds only as long as we keep doing the spiritual work that produced it. Two sentences earlier the book is blunt: 'We are not cured of alcoholism' (page 85). A reprieve is not a pardon. It is a stay, granted for today.

4d0fd5e19826.t: So what is the maintenance the reprieve depends on? The book does not leave us guessing. That sentence sits in the middle of the instructions for Steps Ten and Eleven (pages 84-88). Maintenance means a personal inventory that runs all day, mistakes set right quickly, and prayer and meditation in the morning, at night, and whenever we get rattled in between. The sections below walk through it straight from the text.

7dbcf357366f.t: What Page 85 Is Warning Us About

280a60c5b45f.t: Just before the famous line, the book describes how good recovered life can feel. The problem has been removed. We are not fighting liquor or even avoiding temptation, and we feel as if we had been placed in 'a position of neutrality—safe and protected' (page 85). That new attitude toward liquor arrives without any thought or effort on our part (page 85). Then comes the warning: 'It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. We are headed for trouble if we do, for alcohol is a subtle foe' (page 85). The threat is not that the program stops working. The threat is that we stop working the program because it worked. The neutrality lasts, the book says, 'so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition' (page 85).

6332bf144226.t: Step Ten: The Inventory That Never Stops

aa1654b59b18.t: Maintenance begins on page 84 with Step Ten, which asks us to keep taking personal inventory and to set right new mistakes as we go along (page 84). The instruction is concrete: 'Continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear' (page 84). When these crop up, we ask God at once to remove them, talk them over with someone, and make amends quickly if we have harmed anyone, then turn our thoughts to someone we can help (page 84). This is not a yearly housecleaning. It is a spot-check we run in the middle of ordinary days, and the book says it should continue for our lifetime (page 84). The attitude behind it fits in seven words: 'Love and tolerance of others is our code' (page 84).

6523e58baec3.t: Step Eleven: Morning, Night, and All Through the Day

67d8b3aacc14.t: Page 85 then turns to Step Eleven, prayer and meditation, and pages 86 through 88 lay out a rhythm anyone can follow. At night: 'When we retire at night, we constructively review our day. Were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid?' (page 86). After the review we ask God's forgiveness and what corrective measures should be taken, careful not to slide into worry or morbid reflection (page 86). In the morning: 'On awakening let us think about the twenty-four hours ahead' (page 86), asking God to direct our thinking before the day starts. And in the thick of things: 'As we go through the day we pause, when agitated or doubtful, and ask for the right thought or action' (page 87), reminding ourselves that we are no longer running the show (pages 87-88). The book closes these instructions with a plain reassurance: 'It works—it really does' (page 88).

4c2368426200.t: Why a Daily Reprieve Is Good News

d62769d541cb.t: At first, contingent sobriety can sound like living under a suspended sentence. Read it again and it turns into freedom. We are not asked to stay sober forever. We are asked to maintain our spiritual condition today, and 'Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities' (page 85). The book even calls this kind of effort the proper use of the will (page 85), so we are not passive in it. The maintenance is not a tax added on top of sobriety. It is the same set of actions that made us well, kept warm. Yes, the reprieve is contingent. It is also renewable every single morning, for as long as we are willing to do the simple things pages 84 through 88 describe. We do not have to be cured. We have something that works one day at a time, and today is the only day we are asked to work it.

1d5f75b664d0.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (the Big Book), 4th Edition, chapter 'Into Action', pages 84-88; the daily reprieve sentence is on page 85

2727f4c0a80b.t: What page is the daily reprieve quote on in the Big Book?

4dfefdb595e8.t: Page 85 of Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition, in the chapter Into Action. The full sentence reads: 'What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85). It comes in the discussion of Step Ten, right after the book states, 'We are not cured of alcoholism' (page 85).

693d9756650a.t: What does 'contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' mean?

78024b5c0600.t: It means our sobriety depends on daily spiritual upkeep, not on time accumulated. The Big Book defines that upkeep as Step Ten's continuous personal inventory, watching for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear (page 84), and Step Eleven's prayer and meditation in the morning, at night, and whenever we are agitated or doubtful (pages 86-87). We keep doing today what got us well yesterday.

f9aead3b1195.t: Does the Big Book say alcoholics can be cured?

f511d7eb88f8.t: No. Page 85 says plainly, 'We are not cured of alcoholism.' What we have instead is a daily reprieve that is renewed by maintaining our spiritual condition, and the book warns that alcohol is a subtle foe and that resting on our laurels leads to trouble (page 85).

1e8b10f367b5.t: How do I maintain my spiritual condition every day?

a2cfc0849fce.t: The Big Book gives a simple rhythm on pages 84 through 88. Through the day we watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear and set mistakes right quickly (page 84); on awakening we plan the day and ask God to direct our thinking (page 86); when agitated or doubtful we pause and ask for the right thought or action (page 87); and at night we constructively review our day (page 86).

9dd93b3597cb.t: Big Book Fear Inventory — Step 4, Pages 67-68

33efef4d92b4.t: How the Big Book's fear inventory works: list your fears, ask why you have them, and the remedy on page 68 — trusting God rather than self.

cce3ec67f651.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / The Big Book Fear Inventory

ecb6d659b2a3.t: How the Big Book has us review our fears — and what it offers in their place.

3f08f51aae93.t: The Big Book's fear inventory lives on pages 67 and 68, in Chapter 5, How It Works — a few short paragraphs tucked between the resentment inventory and the review of our relationships. Short, but not small. The book introduces fear with unusual force: 'It was an evil and corroding thread; the fabric of our existence was shot through with it' (page 67). If you have ever gotten honest about what actually drove the drinking — and the lying, the hiding, the big talk — you know why the book gives fear its own review.

832f8ae41696.t: The directions are plainer than we expect. 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper, even though we had no resentment in connection with them' (page 68). That last clause matters. In the resentment inventory we had already noticed fear sitting underneath entry after entry. Here the book has us list the fears that stand on their own — fear of losing a job, a marriage, our health, our standing, fear of being found out, fear of ending up alone. On paper, each one, by name. Fear does its best work in the dark, and the inventory is simply the act of turning the lights on.

6af6e613a9ed.t: Then comes the question that turns a list into an inventory: 'We asked ourselves why we had them. Wasn't it because self-reliance failed us?' (page 68). We had run our lives on our own strength, our own cleverness, our own plans — and the returns kept shrinking. Self-reliance was the strategy, and fear was the receipt. The book allows that self-reliance was good as far as it went, but it didn't go far enough. When the bet is everything and the bankroll is only ourselves, fear is simply honest arithmetic.

b0ec6f5f13b8.t: The fear inventory doesn't end with insight; it ends with a change of ground. 'We are now on a different basis; the basis of trusting and relying upon God' (page 68). Instead of demanding that we be big enough for every threat, we hand the outcome to something bigger than us. The practical prayer is right there in the text: 'We ask Him to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be' (page 68). Notice the direction of that prayer — not toward the thing we're afraid of losing, but toward who we might become. And the book's promise for this piece of work is immediate and modest: 'At once, we commence to outgrow fear' (page 68). Commence. It is a beginning renewed daily, not a lightning cure.

f0c967c2d6ff.t: If you are on Step Four, take a fresh sheet and write down every fear you can name, whether or not it connects to a resentment. Beside each one, ask the book's question: why do I have it? Where did relying on myself alone actually leave me? Then use the prayer on page 68 for each fear on the list, and bring the whole sheet to your sponsor when you share your Fifth Step. Many of us date the real loosening of fear's grip to that one honest conversation. The Promises even circle back to this work later in the book: 'Fear of people and of economic insecurity will leave us' (page 84). The old fears may still knock. The difference is that we no longer have to answer the door alone.

59a53e4e5ea0.t: How do I do a Big Book fear inventory?

Then pray for the fear to be removed and your attention redirected to what God would have you be (page 68), and review the list with your sponsor in Step Five.

The remedy it proposes is a change of basis, from relying on ourselves to trusting God (page 68).

0bd01c837b64.t: Does the fear ever actually leave?

328c7e707b6d.t: The book says we 'commence to outgrow fear' at once (page 68) — a beginning that grows with daily practice. Later, among the Ninth Step Promises, it says plainly: 'Fear of people and of economic insecurity will leave us' (page 84).

384eb05c1938.t: How It Works: Big Book Chapter 5 Explained (Pages 58-60)

873315ad6b26.t: Chapter 5 of the Big Book (pages 58-60) explains how AA works: the famous opening promise, the abc's, and why half measures availed us nothing.

0609a90b52f9.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / How It Works: Chapter 5 of the Big Book

3da625d6796b.t: How It Works: Chapter 5 of the Big Book

b948fc32f31f.t: The words we hear at almost every meeting: pages 58 to 60, taken slowly

a57ad266a66f.t: <0>How It Works</0> is the title of Chapter 5 of <1>Alcoholics Anonymous</1>, the Big Book, and the part most of us know by heart sits on pages 58 through 60. This is the passage read aloud at the start of almost every AA meeting. It opens with one of the most famous sentences in recovery: "Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (page 58). In three short pages the book hands us the whole program in miniature: honesty as the one requirement, willingness to go to any length, the Twelve Steps themselves, and three plain conclusions about our condition and where the help comes from.

603e0770c093.t: So how does it work? Through honesty and thoroughness. Page 58 says the people who do not recover are usually those who "cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program," people who are "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (page 58). Notice what that sentence does not say. It does not say we fail because we are too weak, too far gone, or too bad. The book puts the outcome in our hands: if we can get honest with ourselves and follow the path thoroughly, we recover.

bef9edeafdfa.t: The Promise and the Price on Page 58

31214e8e9328.t: Page 58 asks whether we want what sober members have and whether we are willing to go to any length to get it. Many of us balked at some of the Steps. "We thought we could find an easier, softer way. But we could not" (page 58). So the book pleads with us: "With all the earnestness at our command, we beg of you to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (page 58). Holding on to our old ideas got us nowhere until we let go absolutely. Then comes the reminder of the opponent: alcohol is "cunning, baffling, powerful" (pages 58 and 59), and without help it is too much for us. But there is One who has all power, and the book's whole hope for us fits in five words: "May you find Him now!" (page 59).

d0d2c89f02b0.t: Page 59 gives us the hinge of the chapter: "Half measures availed us nothing. We stood at the turning point. We asked His protection and care with complete abandon" (page 59). Most of us tried the half measures first. We cut down, switched drinks, made promises, worked a Step or two and skipped the uncomfortable ones. The turning point is the moment we admit our own plans have run out and give ourselves to the program completely. Right after that surrender the book says, "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (page 59), and lists all Twelve Steps across pages 59 and 60. Suggested, not commanded. The book never bullies us; it simply reports what worked for the people who wrote it.

cdbf937692c4.t: After the Steps, the book gathers everything into three pertinent ideas, the ones we call the abc's (page 60): <0>(a)</0> "That we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives," <1>(b)</1> "That probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism," and <2>(c)</2> "That God could and would if He were sought" (page 60). The first is Step One in a single line. The second closes the exits we kept trying: willpower alone, the love of our families, our own best thinking. None of it relieved the illness by itself. The third is pure hope, and it is worth reading slowly. It does not say God might help us. It says He could and would, on one condition only: that He be sought.

12ddb016c61f.t: Page 60 also expects our panic. Many of us exclaimed, "What an order! I can't go through with it." The reply is gentle: "Do not be discouraged" (page 60). The book admits that "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (page 60). "We are not saints. The point is, that we are willing to grow along spiritual lines" (page 60). Then comes the sentence many of us lean on every day: "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" (page 60). That is why these pages open our meetings. Not to scold us, but to remind us that the path is walkable. We show up honest, we take the Steps thoroughly, and we let God do for us what we could not do for ourselves.

9b7567bb3f00.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (the Big Book), 4th Edition. Chapter 5, "How It Works," pages 58-71; passage discussed: pages 58-60 (the opening promise, the Twelve Steps, half measures, the abc's, spiritual progress not perfection).

ea56c486c4d4.t: What pages are 'How It Works' in the Big Book?

3f11bbc53f0b.t: Chapter 5, 'How It Works,' begins on page 58 of the 4th Edition, and the portion read aloud at most AA meetings runs from page 58 through the abc's on page 60. The Twelve Steps are listed on pages 59 and 60. The full chapter continues to page 71, where it carries us into Step Four.

cb965b96ee00.t: What are the abc's in the Big Book?

0e35ce41cdc3.t: The abc's are the three pertinent ideas on page 60: (a) that we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives, (b) that probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism, and (c) that God could and would if He were sought. Together they compress the first two Steps into three lines. They come right after the Twelve Steps are listed and sum up everything the book has argued to that point.

fba36b9441fb.t: What does 'half measures availed us nothing' mean?

aaa4f26cf019.t: On page 59 the Big Book says half measures availed us nothing, that we stood at the turning point, and that we asked God's protection and care with complete abandon. It means partial effort at the program got us nowhere; cutting down, bargaining, or working only the comfortable Steps did not relieve our alcoholism. The turning point is choosing to give ourselves to the program completely rather than keeping one foot in the old life.

f41f5c4240de.t: Does 'rarely have we seen a person fail' mean AA never fails?

e41164f1536b.t: It is not a guarantee; it is a report of experience with a condition attached. Page 58 says those who do not recover are usually people who cannot or will not be completely honest with themselves, so the emphasis falls on honesty and thoroughness, not on being flawless. Page 60 balances it by saying we claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection.

c8302ed6afc7.t: More Will Be Revealed: Big Book Meaning (Page 164)

c5fce93576e0.t: More will be revealed comes from page 164 of the Big Book, which says the book is meant to be suggestive only and God will constantly disclose more.

118d7cc71e98.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / More Will Be Revealed: What Page 164 of the Big Book Means

ded98f6327f0.t: More Will Be Revealed: What Page 164 of the Big Book Means

71710ce8131c.t: The last page of the basic text promises that our understanding will keep growing

66d10ff4adcd.t: In recovery, 'more will be revealed' is shorthand for one of the most hopeful promises in the Big Book. It comes from page 164, the very last page of the basic text, where the first members wrote, 'Our book is meant to be suggestive only. We realize we know only a little. God will constantly disclose more to you and to us.' That is the whole idea in three plain sentences. The people who wrote the book were not handing us a finished system. They were handing us a beginning, and they promised that God would keep teaching all of us, writers and readers alike, as we walked forward.

3c4e89d604a6.t: The saying means two things at once. First, humility. Even the founders admitted they knew only a little, so none of us has to pretend we have it all figured out. Second, hope. Our understanding of God, of ourselves, and of this way of living is not stuck at today's level. If we stay sober and keep doing the work, more gets disclosed. The book calls itself suggestive rather than final (page 164), and that leaves room for every one of us to grow past where we started.

9f3ba8eb17f6.t: Here is a detail worth knowing: the exact words 'more will be revealed' do not appear anywhere in the Big Book. The fellowship condensed the page 164 promise into a saying, and it stuck because it names something we all experience. The passage sits in the closing paragraphs of the chapter <0>A Vision For You</0>, at the end of the basic text. Right after promising that God will constantly disclose more, the book gives us a job. It says, 'Ask Him in your morning meditation what you can do each day for the man who is still sick.' Then it adds, 'The answers will come, if your own house is in order.' Revelation and action travel together. We do not receive more light by sitting still. We receive it by praying, cleaning house, and helping the next alcoholic (page 164).

a5a8df3e25da.t: Calling the book suggestive was a deliberate act of humility, and it protects us from turning the program into a rigid rulebook. The same spirit shows up on page 60, where the book says, 'We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection.' The Steps are offered there as guides to progress, and the book admits that no one among us has maintained anything like perfect adherence to these principles (page 60). If the founders could say they knew only a little, we can say it too. That admission keeps us teachable, and teachable people stay sober.

7e6faa3f7026.t: It also matters because our reprieve is daily. Page 85 reminds us that we are not cured of alcoholism; what we really have is 'a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition.' A daily reprieve calls for daily growth. If the book had claimed to be the final word, we might read it once and coast. Because it claims to be suggestive only, we keep coming back, to the text and to God, for the next lesson.

541737ccc909.t: How More Gets Revealed in Practice

43d837f2ff1c.t: The disclosure is gradual, and the book says so. Describing life after Step Ten, page 84 tells us our next function is to grow in understanding and effectiveness, and that 'This is not an overnight matter. It should continue for our lifetime.' We work the Steps, we pray and meditate, we keep our side of the street clean, and understanding arrives on God's schedule rather than ours. Most of us can see it when we look back. Page 100 says we realize that 'the things which came to us when we put ourselves in God's hands were better than anything we could have planned.'

24db4b4b2d8d.t: So when an old-timer smiles and says more will be revealed, they are not brushing us off. They are handing us the last page of the basic text, in spirit if not in letter. The God of our understanding is still teaching, the program we know today is not the ceiling, and our part is the willingness, honesty, and open-mindedness that Appendix II names as essentials (page 568). We show up for morning meditation, we keep our house in order, we give freely of what we find. The book closes by promising that 'you will surely meet some of us as you trudge the Road of Happy Destiny' (page 164). More will be revealed on that road. It always is.

cad8dc21cbff.t: Where does 'more will be revealed' come from in the Big Book?

We realize we know only a little. God will constantly disclose more to you and to us.' Members shortened that promise into the saying we hear at meetings.

49a9a0be044a.t: What does 'more will be revealed' mean in AA?

952b8abdb1b8.t: It means our understanding keeps growing as long as we keep working the program. The founders admitted they knew only a little and promised that God would constantly disclose more (page 164). Since the book claims spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection (page 60), nobody graduates; we all stay students.

Page 84 adds that growing in understanding is not an overnight matter but a lifetime practice, so we keep working the Steps one day at a time.

The LONG FORM — the fuller original wording, and the one worth reading — is on pages 563–566. The Twelve Concepts follow on pages 574–575. Nearly every summary online quotes only the short form, which is why so much of what circulates is incomplete. 271ec6ee3445.t: No. The Twelve Traditions are governance, not theology. They bind A.A. groups and the Fellowship as a whole — not individual members, and not independent businesses or outside organisations. They were adopted in 1950 to keep A.A. from being owned, co-opted, or torn apart by disputes over money, property and authority. They are not a rulebook for a member's personal life.

435f000c57be.t: Big Book Page 83: The Promises and Living the Spiritual Life

aba443637c6e.t: Page 83 of the Big Book holds the start of the Promises and the famous line that the spiritual life is not a theory. Learn what this page really says.

647ceb1589c4.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Big Book Page 83: Where the Promises Begin

a02957f50ff4.t: Big Book Page 83: Where the Promises Begin

21dc92253f88.t: One page from Into Action that gets read aloud in meetings all over the world.

851c5e1120ca.t: Page 83 of the Big Book (Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition) may be the most quoted page in the whole book. It sits in the chapter <0>Into Action</0>, right in the heart of Step Nine, and it carries two treasures. The first is the line so many of us have underlined: 'The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it.' (page 83). The second is the beginning of the Ninth Step Promises, which open at the bottom of the page: 'If we are painstaking about this phase of our development, we will be amazed before we are half way through' (page 83).

24d471f9b0aa.t: Those Promises are the words countless groups read aloud at meetings. 'We are going to know a new freedom and a new happiness. We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' (page 83). They run from the bottom of page 83 onto page 84, and they describe, plainly and specifically, what begins to happen in us when we do the work of making amends. If you searched for page 83, you probably heard one of these lines somewhere and wanted to find its home. This is it.

0bd4748408a7.t: Context matters here. Page 83 is about making amends to the people closest to us, especially our families. The page just before it compares the alcoholic to a tornado roaring through the lives of others (page 82), and page 83 answers the alcoholic who thinks that simply staying sober is enough. The book tells of a farmer who climbs out of his cyclone cellar, finds his home ruined, and cheerfully remarks that at least the wind stopped blowing (page 82). That is us if we get sober and never repair the damage. So the book is blunt with us: 'Yes, there is a long period of reconstruction ahead' (page 83). We take the lead. A mumbled apology will not fill the bill. We sit down with the family, look honestly at the past without criticizing them, and ask each morning that our Creator show us the way of 'patience, tolerance, kindliness and love' (page 83).

c33d4a7a5b9d.t: The Spiritual Life Is Not a Theory

0886c4aecc85.t: Right in the middle of that family discussion comes the sentence that made this page famous: 'The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it.' (page 83). The book applies it immediately. We should not preach spiritual matters at our families or push the program on them. They will change in time, because our behavior will convince them more than our words ever could (page 83). Many of us call this a living amends. We stop announcing that we are different and start being different, one ordinary day at a time. Page 83 is where the Big Book tells us that amends are something we live, not something we say.

cab5689b363d.t: Where the Promises Begin, and What They Ask of Us

15c96ab78228.t: Notice that the Promises open with a condition. 'If we are painstaking about this phase of our development' (page 83) points straight back at the amends work described above. The Promises are not attached to mere sobriety; they are attached to Step Nine. Then comes the sweep of them: a new freedom, a new happiness, and the assurance that 'We will comprehend the word serenity and we will know peace' (page 83). They continue onto page 84, where the book anticipates our doubt: 'Are these extravagant promises? We think not.' (page 84). They come 'sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly' (page 84), and 'They will always materialize if we work for them' (page 84). That last line is the quiet engine of the whole passage. The Promises are a description of results, and the work is ours to do.

e1898f5bf6a8.t: We do not have to rebuild everything today. The Big Book reminds us two pages later that what we really have is a 'daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85). So today we can take the lead in one small act of reconstruction: a kind word where we used to criticize, showing up where we used to disappear, sweeping our side of the street without inspecting anyone else's. Bring page 83 to your sponsor or your group and talk it through. Read it slowly, out loud if you can. The spiritual life is not a theory, and neither is this page. We live it, and the Promises begin to come true.

We have to live it.'; the Ninth Step Promises begin); page 84 (the Promises conclude; 'Are these extravagant promises? We think not.'); page 85 (daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition).

4e68cfd12bb3.t: Powerless Over Alcohol: Step 1 in the Big Book Explained

2d2b9a9c6a60.t: The Big Book says we lost the power of choice in drink (page 24). Step 1 powerlessness, the allergy and obsession, and pages 30-43, explained simply.

4858da4767db.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Powerless Over Alcohol: What Step 1 Really Means

029a2f3faed5.t: Powerless Over Alcohol: What Step 1 Really Means

c16841dbe8ea.t: An allergy of the body, an obsession of the mind, and the honest admission that sets us free

1ce200d34e80.t: When the Big Book talks about being powerless over alcohol, it means something far more specific than weak willpower. Step One reads, 'We admitted we were powerless over alcohol—that our lives had become unmanageable' (page 59). The book describes a twofold condition: a body that reacts abnormally to alcohol once we start drinking, and a mind that keeps talking us into the first drink no matter what we swore last time. Page 24 says it plainly: 'The fact is that most alcoholics, for reasons yet obscure, have lost the power of choice in drink.' That lost power of choice is what powerlessness means.

4e4cafee6a4f.t: This is why trying harder never worked for us. If the problem were only in the body, we could simply stay away from the first drink. If it were only in the mind, we could stop after one or two. We have both. Once we start we cannot stop, and once we stop we cannot stay stopped on our own. Admitting that is Step 1, and the Big Book treats it as the foundation everything else rests on.

38d1c6238d00.t: The Doctor's Opinion: An Allergy of the Body

61fee0527525.t: The book opens with a letter from Dr. William D. Silkworth, a physician who treated thousands of alcoholics. He suggests that the action of alcohol on chronic alcoholics is a manifestation of an allergy, and that the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class of drinkers and never occurs in the average temperate drinker (page xxviii). In other words, our bodies do something with alcohol that a normal drinker's body does not. Once the first drink goes down, a craving rises that demands more, and willpower has almost nothing to say about it. The doctor saw that these men could not start drinking without the craving developing, and that the only relief he could suggest was entire abstinence (page xxx). The practical lesson is simple. For people like us, the problem is never the fifth drink. It is the first.

bb4fe88ff26c.t: An allergy alone would not defeat anyone, because we could just avoid the substance. The chapter More About Alcoholism names the part of us that will not let that happen: 'The idea that somehow, someday he will control and enjoy his drinking is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker' (page 30). The book calls the persistence of this illusion astonishing, and says many of us pursue it to the gates of insanity or death (page 30). Then it shows the obsession at work. A man of thirty quit for twenty-five years, drank in retirement, and was in a hospital within two months (pages 32-33). Jim, the car salesman, drank whiskey mixed with milk on the strange notion that a full stomach would protect him (pages 35-36). Fred, the accountant, had every reason to stay sober and simply decided a couple of cocktails with dinner would do no harm (pages 39-41).

d6e275272ee7.t: The point of every story is the same. At the critical moment, the mind does not defend us. 'The alcoholic at certain times has no effective mental defense against the first drink' (page 43). The book adds that neither we nor any other human being can provide that defense; it must come from a Higher Power (page 43).

74ce3589b108.t: The Big Book never pronounces anyone alcoholic. It hands us the evidence and lets us diagnose ourselves. It suggests trying some controlled drinking, trying to drink and stop abruptly, more than once, and being honest about the result (pages 31-32). The next chapter opens with the clearest test in the book: 'If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely, or if when drinking, you have little control over the amount you take, you are probably alcoholic' (page 44). And it tells us what real acceptance looks like: 'We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics. This is the first step in recovery' (page 30). The delusion that we are like other people has to be smashed (page 30).

8b6e947d78a9.t: Why Powerlessness Is the Beginning of Hope

086b737e30bd.t: Admitting powerlessness sounds like defeat, but in the Big Book it is the doorway to everything good that follows. Lack of power was exactly our dilemma, and the main object of the book is to help us find a Power greater than ourselves that will solve our problem (page 45). We finally stop fighting a battle we have lost a hundred times and become teachable. This page is a study companion for the text, not medical advice; questions about detox or withdrawal belong with a doctor. For today, the admission is enough. We concede to our innermost selves that alcohol has us beaten, and in that honest moment, recovery begins.

fdb4edef7ff1.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition: The Doctor's Opinion (pp. xxv-xxxii); There Is a Solution (pp. 17-29, esp. p. 24); More About Alcoholism (pp. 30-43); We Agnostics (pp. 44-45); How It Works (p. 59, Step One)

4d74654cb3fc.t: What does 'powerless over alcohol' mean in the Big Book?

cca68fceae7c.t: It means we have lost the power of choice in drink (page 24). The Big Book describes a physical allergy that triggers craving once we start drinking (page xxviii) and a mental obsession that leads us back to the first drink when we are sober (page 30). Together they explain why willpower alone never held for us.

cc354eb04e33.t: Where does the Big Book explain Step 1?

55c5ecaa9b30.t: The words of Step One appear on page 59, but the case for powerlessness is built in The Doctor's Opinion (pages xxv-xxxii) and the chapter More About Alcoholism (pages 30-43). Those pages cover the great obsession, the stories of Jim and Fred, and the statement that the alcoholic has no effective mental defense against the first drink (page 43).

59706963961e.t: How do I know if I'm powerless over alcohol?

a1056b633f9e.t: The Big Book says only we can decide for ourselves, and it offers a test: try some controlled drinking, more than once, and be honest about the result (pages 31-32). Page 44 gives the clearest measure: if you cannot quit entirely when you honestly want to, or have little control over the amount once you start, you are probably alcoholic. This is self-reflection with the text, not a medical evaluation.

6f70044a6cb3.t: Why is admitting powerlessness the first step in recovery?

3d2ac0536e1a.t: Because the Big Book says we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics before anything else could work (page 30). Since no human power can provide a defense against the first drink, admitting powerlessness is what opens us to the Higher Power that can (pages 43 and 45).

0924c4480144.t: What Does the Big Book Say About Resentment? (Pages 64-67)

5489d5aa806f.t: The Big Book calls resentment the 'number one' offender (page 64). Learn the resentment inventory of pages 64-67 and the freedom on the other side.

fa5d5c8e4ceb.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / What Does the Big Book Say About Resentment?

2116f0af78a9.t: What Does the Big Book Say About Resentment?

5c3b1be00c29.t: The number one offender, the inventory that names it, and the freedom waiting on page 67.

5a3b735954bb.t: When someone asks what the Big Book says about resentment, the answer starts on page 64, and it does not mince words. The book calls resentment the 'number one' offender and says it 'destroys more alcoholics than anything else' (page 64). That is a strong claim. Not fear, not money troubles, not even the drink itself, but resentment sits at the top of the list. The reason follows in the same passage: 'From it stem all forms of spiritual disease, for we have been not only mentally and physically ill, we have been spiritually sick' (page 64). For people like us, whose recovery depends on a spiritual experience, resentment is not just a bad mood. It is a threat to our sobriety.

3b5bb5dbf162.t: The good news is that the Big Book does not stop at the diagnosis. Pages 64 through 67 lay out a practical method for dealing with it: a written inventory that sets our resentments on paper, a new way of seeing the people who hurt us, and a turn toward our own part in the story. Page 66 sums up why the work matters: 'It is plain that a life which includes deep resentment leads only to futility and unhappiness.' We do this work to get free.

4b92b9baf587.t: Why Resentment Is the Number One Offender

d64466148e91.t: Page 66 explains the danger in words many of us have underlined. When we harbor deep resentment, 'we shut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit' (page 66). Other people may be able to afford a grudge; the book says these things may be 'the dubious luxury of normal men, but for alcoholics these things are poison' (page 66). When we are spiritually blocked, the insanity of alcohol returns, and for us that is a matter of life and death. That is why the book is so blunt: 'If we were to live, we had to be free of anger' (page 66). This is not a moral lecture. It is a survival instruction.

5fdf151d1723.t: The Inventory: Setting Resentments on Paper

edcfe95f3182.t: The method begins simply. 'In dealing with resentments, we set them on paper. We listed people, institutions or principles with whom we were angry' (page 64). That is the first column: who or what we resent. In the second column we wrote the cause, the specific thing that happened. In the third, the book has us ask what part of us was affected, and page 65 shows a sample grid where each resentment touches our self-esteem, our security, our ambitions, or our personal and sex relations. Seeing our anger laid out this way, most of us notice something humbling. The list turns out to be a map of the places we feel threatened.

aba582ca0367.t: Then comes the turn that changes everything. 'Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes' (page 67). The book gives us searching questions: 'Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?' (page 67). This is not about excusing anyone who harmed us. It is about finding the one part of the story we can actually do something about, which is our part.

daa1f2c579ac.t: How the Book Says We Get Free

d29676c3bf50.t: Before we ever reach our own mistakes, the Big Book hands us a new pair of glasses. It suggests we regard the people who wronged us as perhaps spiritually sick, just as we were (pages 66-67). Then it gives us a prayer: we asked God to help us show them 'the same tolerance, pity, and patience that we would cheerfully grant a sick friend' (page 67). When someone offends us, the book even gives us words to say: 'This is a sick man. How can I be helpful to him? God save me from being angry. Thy will be done' (page 67). We avoid retaliation or argument, the book adds, because we would not treat sick people that way (page 67). None of this means what happened to us was okay. It means we stop drinking the poison ourselves.

8b8c19dc91f9.t: The Freedom on the Other Side

889ff48abe84.t: What waits past this work is the whole point. The resentment inventory carries us into Steps Five through Nine, and the promises on that road are specific: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' (page 83). The Big Book's teaching on resentment comes down to this: we cannot afford it, we can write our way out of it, and God can remove what we could never argue ourselves out of. Many of us walked into the Fourth Step certain our anger was justified, and walked out seeing that justified or not, it was killing us. Letting it go was not weakness. It was the door to a life where yesterday's injuries no longer decide today's peace.

d54d5a959118.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: 'How It Works,' pages 64-67 (resentment as the number one offender, the resentment inventory, the spiritually sick perspective, the turn to our own mistakes); 'Into Action,' page 83 (the promise of not regretting the past).

ab91a88c0ad3.t: What page does the Big Book call resentment the number one offender?

c66f3e1aa196.t: Page 64, in the chapter How It Works. The Big Book says resentment is the 'number one' offender and that it destroys more alcoholics than anything else (page 64). The full discussion of resentment, including the written inventory, runs from page 64 through page 67.

ba3003e2e654.t: What are the columns in the Big Book resentment inventory?

91b9e64ce656.t: The instructions begin on page 64, and page 65 shows a written grid. The first column lists the people, institutions, or principles we are angry with, the second lists the cause, and the third asks which part of self was affected, such as self-esteem, security, ambitions, or personal and sex relations. Then on page 67 the book turns the inventory around and asks where we had been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking, and frightened.

9d7f96fde711.t: How does the Big Book say to get rid of resentment?

32e7028445d7.t: It suggests we regard the people who wronged us as spiritually sick, just as we were (pages 66-67). We ask God to help us show them the same tolerance, pity, and patience we would grant a sick friend (page 67), we avoid retaliation or argument, and we look for our own mistakes instead of dwelling on the wrongs of others (page 67). Freedom comes from prayer and honest inventory, not from winning the argument.

4e1c948cb799.t: Why is resentment so dangerous for alcoholics?

43eaf252786c.t: Because it blocks the spiritual experience that keeps us sober. Page 66 says that when we harbor deep resentment we shut ourselves off from the sunlight of the Spirit, and that anger may be a luxury other people can afford but for alcoholics it is poison. The stakes for us are sobriety itself, which is why the book says that if we were to live, we had to be free of anger (page 66).

c7b3677cfc8b.t: Self-Will Run Riot: What the Big Book Says on Page 62

e2b7dfc7a65b.t: Self-will run riot appears on page 62 of the Big Book. Learn what the phrase means, who the actor on page 60 is, and how Step Three offers the way out.

66eb4b13eacf.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Self-Will Run Riot in the Big Book

a74fda276b04.t: Self-Will Run Riot in the Big Book

9a2d862b7310.t: Understanding pages 60 to 62, the actor who runs the show, and the root of our troubles

b22fa356a6e9.t: The phrase 'self-will run riot' comes from page 62 of the Big Book, in the chapter How It Works. The full sentence tells us that 'the alcoholic is an extreme example of self-will run riot, though he usually doesn't think so' (page 62). Self-will run riot means a life powered entirely by our own plans, our own demands, and our own ideas of how everyone around us should behave, with nothing to check any of it. To run riot is to run wild. We wanted what we wanted, we pushed until we got it, and we usually could not see that we were the ones doing the pushing.

720183cc44d9.t: The Big Book does not leave the diagnosis vague. Just before that sentence it delivers the verdict: 'Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles' (page 62). Then it adds, 'So our troubles, we think, are basically of our own making' (page 62). That can sound harsh at first, but it may be the most hopeful idea in the whole chapter. If our troubles came from other people, we would have to fix other people. Because they arise in us, the repair can happen in us. The rest of the book is a set of directions for exactly that repair.

cf35bba2d51e.t: The Actor Who Wants to Run the Whole Show

e5a6ca981b54.t: To show us what self-will looks like from the outside, the Big Book paints a picture on pages 60 and 61. Each of us is like an actor who wants to run the whole show, forever trying to arrange the lights, the scenery, and the other players to suit himself. If only our arrangements would stay put, if only people would do as we wished, the show would be great and everybody would be pleased. The first requirement of Step Three is to be convinced that 'any life run on self-will can hardly be a success' (page 60).

eae514499637.t: The book is careful to say the actor is not always a villain. Sometimes he is kind and patient, sometimes he is mean and dishonest, and often his motives are genuinely good (pages 60-61). But the show still does not come off. So he tries harder, and when life still refuses to cooperate he becomes angry, indignant, and full of self-pity, blaming everyone but himself (page 61). The book then asks a question that stings a little: even at his best, is he not producing confusion rather than harmony (page 61)?

a2e2a1a1f60c.t: Selfishness and Self-Centeredness, the Root of Our Troubles

f939b21aa495.t: Page 62 goes on: 'Driven by a hundred forms of fear, self-delusion, self-seeking, and self-pity, we step on the toes of our fellows and they retaliate.' Notice the first word on that list. Our selfishness was never strength; it was fear wearing a costume. Sometimes we seemed to be hurt without any provocation at all, but the book says we invariably found that some earlier decision, based on self, had placed us in a position to be hurt (page 62).

e4a22f7b664c.t: Then the book raises the stakes: 'Above everything, we alcoholics must be rid of this selfishness. We must, or it kills us!' (page 62). That is life-and-death language on purpose, because a self-centered life keeps producing the very pain we drank to escape. The book is just as honest about the limits of willpower. We could not reduce our self-centeredness much by wishing or by trying on our own power; we had to have God's help (page 62).

4bc1de3f9156.t: Quitting the Job of Playing God

f7d2392ee066.t: The way out begins with a resignation. 'First of all, we had to quit playing God. It didn't work' (page 62). Then comes a new arrangement: 'Next, we decided that hereafter in this drama of life, God was going to be our Director' (page 62). Notice that we do not leave the stage. We keep our part; we simply stop trying to direct everyone else's. That decision is Step Three, and the book says that when we sincerely took such a position, remarkable things followed, and we became less interested in ourselves and more interested in what we could contribute to life (page 63).

66c93dc6edc4.t: The Third Step Prayer on page 63 asks God to 'Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will' (page 63). Bondage is the right word. The Big Book treats self-will not as a privilege we surrender but as a prison we get released from, and the release is renewed daily. On pages 87 and 88 the book tells us to pause when agitated or doubtful, ask for the right thought or action, and remind ourselves that we are no longer running the show. That is the actor image coming back around: we play our part, do the next right thing, and let the Director handle the plot.

fef13c7da860.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: pages 60-63, Chapter 5 How It Works (Step Three discussion, the actor illustration, selfishness/self-centeredness as the root of our troubles, self-will run riot, quitting playing God, the Third Step Prayer); pages 87-88, Chapter 6 Into Action (the daily pause, no longer running the show).

40f150f334b6.t: What page is 'self-will run riot' on in the Big Book?

9e9010f0c4c1.t: It appears on page 62 of Alcoholics Anonymous, in Chapter 5, How It Works. The sentence says that 'the alcoholic is an extreme example of self-will run riot, though he usually doesn't think so' (page 62). It comes at the end of the actor illustration that begins on page 60.

19c9c34dde20.t: What does self-will run riot actually mean?

4a5715db8837.t: It means a life run entirely on our own willpower and plans, trying to force people and events to go our way. The Big Book says 'any life run on self-will can hardly be a success' (page 60). To run riot means to run wild and unchecked, which is exactly how our self-will behaved before recovery.

ab644d2ded89.t: Is the Big Book saying my troubles are all my fault?

dd591da0e171.t: Page 62 says our troubles are basically of our own making, but this is a diagnosis, not a condemnation. The same page says our selfishness is driven by a hundred forms of fear, so the book treats us as sick people getting well, not bad people being scolded. The hopeful part is that if the trouble arises in us, then with God's help the change can happen in us too (page 62).

22f3448ba832.t: How do I stop running on self-will?

60331689657c.t: The Big Book's answer is Step Three. 'First of all, we had to quit playing God. It didn't work' (page 62). We decide to let God direct the show instead, take the Third Step Prayer on page 63, and keep the decision fresh each day by pausing when agitated or doubtful and asking for the right thought or action (pages 87-88).

a0a66fa1cd85.t: Big Book Spiritual Experience Appendix II (Pages 567-568)

340a06aca836.t: Appendix II of the Big Book (pages 567-568) explains sudden and educational spiritual experiences and the personality change sufficient for recovery.

1f131443abcb.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / The Spiritual Experience Appendix of the Big Book

a12f729a5114.t: The Spiritual Experience Appendix of the Big Book

9a41e5894784.t: Appendix II, pages 567 and 568: sudden or slow, the change is what counts

3a88ce29b185.t: The spiritual experience appendix of the Big Book is Appendix II, found on pages 567 and 568 of <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, Fourth Edition. It was added after the first printing because many readers came away believing that recovery required a sudden, dramatic encounter with God, and some were quietly giving up when nothing like that happened to them. The appendix settles the question. What the book actually calls for is a 'personality change sufficient to bring about recovery from alcoholism' (page 567), and that change shows up among us in many different forms.

678a993c6c98.t: The appendix names two broad varieties. Some of us have the quick, dramatic kind, the 'sudden and spectacular upheavals' described in the book's first chapters (page 567). Most of us have what the psychologist William James calls the 'educational variety' (page 567), a change that develops slowly over a period of time. To the fear that only the lightning-bolt kind is real, the appendix answers plainly: 'Happily for everyone, this conclusion is erroneous' (page 567). Slow counts. Gradual counts. If we are changing, we are having the experience.

0ff74dc6c670.t: When the Big Book was first published in 1939, stories like Bill's sudden hospital experience left a powerful impression. Many alcoholics concluded that they had to receive an immediate, overwhelming awareness of God, with their whole outlook transformed on the spot, or they were not really recovering (page 567). We can imagine what that belief did to the newcomer who prayed, worked the Steps, and felt no thunder. So the appendix was written to lift that burden, and the book itself expects us to need it; a footnote on page 25 sends the reader straight to Appendix II for the full explanation. Sudden transformations happen, and they happen often, but the appendix says they are by no means the rule (page 567). Nobody is disqualified for waking up slowly.

4349de745079.t: Sudden or Slow: The Educational Variety

bdb80f69060c.t: The educational variety is so gradual that we are usually the last to notice it. The appendix observes that friends of the newcomer often see the difference in him long before he sees it himself (page 567). Then one day he realizes that his whole way of reacting to life has changed, and that he could hardly have brought that about alone. What takes place in a few months of this work, the appendix says, could seldom have been accomplished by years of self-discipline (page 567). That is the quiet miracle most of us live. We stop wanting to drink, we start telling the truth, and the people around us see it first. Page 25 calls this the great fact for us: 'deep and effective spiritual experiences which have revolutionized our whole attitude toward life, toward our fellows and toward God's universe' (page 25).

9413f22f900a.t: The Personality Change Sufficient to Recover

0f177a3646a2.t: Whatever the pace, the substance is the same. The appendix tells us that with few exceptions, members discover an inner resource they never suspected they had, and they come to identify it with their own conception of a Power greater than themselves (pages 567-568). Most of us regard that awareness as the essence of spiritual experience, and our more religious members call it 'God-consciousness' (page 568). Notice how this matches Step Twelve: 'Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps' (page 60). The awakening is the <0>result</0> of the work, not the entrance fee. We do not wait until we feel spiritual to begin; we begin, and the change comes. And since what we really have is a 'daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85), the experience is not a trophy we win once. It is a condition we keep by continuing to grow.

7678571c97c2.t: What the Book Asks of Us

17aaa43f4819.t: The appendix closes with remarkable generosity. It says most emphatically that any alcoholic capable of honestly facing his problems in the light of our experience can recover, provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts. The only thing that can defeat him is an attitude of 'intolerance or belligerent denial' (page 568). Then it hands us the short list: 'Willingness, honesty and open mindedness are the essentials of recovery. But these are indispensable' (page 568). We do not have to believe anything in particular today. We only have to stay open. The appendix ends with Herbert Spencer's warning against 'contempt prior to investigation' (page 568), the one attitude that can keep a person in everlasting ignorance. If we refuse to slam that door, then sudden or slow, loud or quiet, the change will come. And the appendix promises it is enough to recover.

ee80fc47704e.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition: Appendix II, 'Spiritual Experience,' pages 567-568; 'There Is a Solution,' page 25 (including the footnote pointing to Appendix II); 'How It Works,' page 60 (Step Twelve); 'Into Action,' page 85.

46dd162ef6e3.t: What page is the spiritual experience appendix in the Big Book?

894102de8d2e.t: Appendix II, titled Spiritual Experience, is on pages 567 and 568 of the Fourth Edition of Alcoholics Anonymous. It was added after the first printing because many readers thought recovery required a sudden, dramatic experience of God. The appendix explains that most experiences are gradual, the kind William James calls the 'educational variety' (page 567).

ece1c7557ab8.t: What is the difference between a sudden spiritual experience and the educational variety?

cf3589a1cdf7.t: A sudden experience is a fast, dramatic upheaval like the ones described in the Big Book's early chapters, while the educational variety develops slowly over a period of time (page 567). The appendix says sudden transformations are frequent but by no means the rule. Both kinds produce the same result: a personality change sufficient to bring about recovery from alcoholism (page 567).

6f0ad700d656.t: Do I have to believe in God to have a spiritual experience in AA?

7c5f5df949e6.t: The appendix says any alcoholic capable of honestly facing his problems can recover, provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts (page 568). We start with our own conception of a Power greater than ourselves (pages 567-568), and the book names willingness, honesty, and open-mindedness as the essentials of recovery (page 568).

759b12c6a809.t: What does a personality change sufficient to bring about recovery mean?

c013bf04e6ea.t: It is the appendix's plain description of what a spiritual awakening really is: a change deep enough that we recover from alcoholism (page 567). It may come suddenly or unfold over months, and the people around us often notice it before we do (page 567). Step Twelve describes the same thing as a spiritual awakening that comes as the result of working the Steps (page 60).
