6b463100e427.t: What Does the Big Book Say About Sponsorship?

3bd319300beb.t: The Big Book rarely says 'sponsor.' Chapter 7, Working With Others (pages 89-103), holds the practice: one alcoholic carrying the message to another.

d61594fb24db.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / What Does the Big Book Say About Sponsorship?

87c4b145d08f.t: Working With Others: how carrying the message became what we call sponsorship

8a25328f8586.t: The word 'sponsor' barely appears in the first 164 pages of the Big Book. That surprises a lot of us, because sponsorship feels like the backbone of AA life. But the practice itself is right there, laid out in detail in Chapter 7, 'Working With Others' (pages 89-103). The chapter opens with one of the most quoted promises in the book: 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics. It works when other activities fail' (page 89). That is sponsorship in a single sentence. One alcoholic who has recovered sits down with one who is still suffering and passes on what was freely given to him.

803604afb6c7.t: The practice flows straight out of Step Twelve: 'Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs' (page 60). Chapter 7 names it plainly: 'This is our twelfth suggestion: Carry this message to other alcoholics!' (page 89). So the honest answer to our question is this: the Big Book never describes a title or an office. It describes an action. Sponsorship is simply the name the fellowship later gave to Step Twelve work done one alcoholic to another, over time and with love.

c1baa88513a3.t: The book is plain about why we do this: it keeps us sober. 'Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery' (page 97). Earlier it goes even further: 'Our very lives, as ex-problem drinkers, depend upon our constant thought of others and how we may help meet their needs' (page 20). This is why sponsorship is never a favor the sponsor grants. When the book tells us to explain the program to a newcomer, it adds, 'Actually, he may be helping you more than you are helping him' (page 94). Chapter 6 closes with the line that sets all of this up: 'Faith without works is dead' (page 88). We stay well by giving away what we found.

7e3a01c8ce36.t: How the Big Book Says to Sponsor Someone

aa27038db825.t: Pages 89 through 96 read like a field manual. We are told to cooperate with doctors and ministers and never criticize, because 'To be helpful is our only aim' (page 89). We are told not to chase the unwilling: 'If he does not want to stop drinking, don't waste time trying to persuade him' (page 90). When the newcomer is ready to listen, our instructions are simple: 'Tell him exactly what happened to you. Stress the spiritual feature freely' (page 93). We share experience, not lectures. The book warns us to 'Never talk down to an alcoholic from any moral or spiritual hilltop; simply lay out the kit of spiritual tools for his inspection' (page 95). And it keeps us humble about our own answers: 'We have no monopoly on God; we merely have an approach that worked with us' (page 95).

22799a17df3b.t: A Sponsor Points to God, Not to Himself

00113e8d6a99.t: Chapter 7 draws one boundary that every sponsor and every newcomer needs to hear. The relationship is a bridge, not a crutch. The book says 'we simply do not stop drinking so long as we place dependence upon other people ahead of dependence on God' (page 98). Then comes the strongest sentence in the chapter: 'Burn the idea into the consciousness of every man that he can get well regardless of anyone. The only condition is that he trust in God and clean house' (page 98). A good sponsor takes us through the Steps and then steps out of the way, pointing past himself to the Power that actually does the healing. Our job, the book says, is to 'be at the place where you may be of maximum helpfulness to others' (page 102).

9a38bfc0d85f.t: So if we are new, we look for someone who has recovered through these Steps and ask them to take us through the book, page by page. If we have some sobriety, the message is even simpler: this work is not extra credit. It is the program's own protection plan, and it comes with a promise. Watching people recover, watching loneliness vanish, and watching a fellowship grow up around us is, the book says, 'an experience you must not miss' (page 89). Frequent contact with newcomers is called 'the bright spot of our lives' (page 89). We carry the message today, and the message carries us.

20a098f89527.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition. Primary: Chapter 7, 'Working With Others,' pp. 89-103 (cited: 89, 90, 93, 94, 95, 97, 98, 102). Also: Step Twelve, p. 60 ('How It Works'); p. 88 ('Into Action'); p. 20 ('There Is a Solution').

ed0ea37d6f2d.t: Does the Big Book actually use the word sponsor?

28ca1eb46470.t: Hardly at all in the basic text. What we now call sponsorship comes from Step Twelve (page 60) and Chapter 7, Working With Others (pages 89-103), which give detailed instructions for one alcoholic carrying the message to another. The word came later from AA practice; the action was there from the beginning.

24a03edec102.t: What chapter of the Big Book is about sponsorship?

73afe1679516.t: Chapter 7, Working With Others, pages 89 through 103. It opens by promising that nothing insures immunity from drinking like intensive work with other alcoholics (page 89), then walks through exactly how to approach, talk with, and guide a newcomer.

23d8d847aa44.t: Do I need a sponsor to work the Steps according to the Big Book?

e56b613becd1.t: The Big Book never makes a sponsor a formal requirement, but its whole design assumes the Steps are passed from one alcoholic to another; that is what Chapter 7 describes (pages 89-103). It also reminds us the newcomer can get well regardless of anyone if he trusts God and cleans house (page 98). Most of us find that a sponsor is simply how the book's plan works in daily life.

eb627e5b27ff.t: What does the Big Book say a sponsor should do?

f2ce8122cdd1.t: Tell the newcomer exactly what happened to them and stress the spiritual side (page 93), lay out the kit of spiritual tools without preaching from any hilltop (page 95), and point the newcomer to God rather than to themselves (page 98). The book says this work protects the sponsor's own sobriety too (pages 89 and 97).

26af023b068b.t: Big Book Step 4 Instructions: Pages 63-71 Explained

decd9fdadda9.t: The Big Book gives its Step 4 instructions on pages 63-71, covering the resentment, fear, and sex inventories, and this guide walks through each one.

90dffcfb3c63.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / Big Book Step 4 Instructions: The Three Inventories

a40f0b041f7a.t: Big Book Step 4 Instructions: The Three Inventories

2cf2cd7f6ccf.t: What pages 63 to 71 actually tell us to write about resentments, fears, and sex conduct.

63151600ca07.t: If we are looking for the actual Step 4 instructions in the Big Book, they run from the bottom of page 63 through page 71 in Chapter 5, How It Works. After the Third Step decision, the book says we launched out on a course of vigorous action, a personal housecleaning many of us had never attempted (page 63). The inventory itself is three written lists: a <0>resentment inventory</0> (pages 64 to 67), a <1>fear inventory</1> (pages 67 to 68), and a <2>review of our sex conduct</2> (pages 68 to 70). That is the whole assignment. The book never asks for a life story or a catalog of every sin we can remember; it asks for an honest, written look at what has been blocking us.

bd823adc8587.t: The book opens with a plain business picture: 'A business which takes no regular inventory usually goes broke' (page 64). So we took stock honestly, searching out the flaws in our make-up that caused our failure, convinced that self in its various forms is what had defeated us (page 64).

a12887ddcc64.t: The Big Book calls resentment the 'number one' offender and says 'It destroys more alcoholics than anything else' (page 64). So the inventory begins there. 'In dealing with resentments, we set them on paper' (page 64). We list the people, institutions, and principles we are angry with. Beside each name we write the cause, the specific thing that happened. Then we ask which part of self was hurt or threatened: our self-esteem, our security, our ambitions, our personal or sex relations (pages 64 and 65). Page 65 even shows a sample grid so we can see exactly what a finished list looks like.

887efe638081.t: Then comes the turn. Reading the list over, we see the price we have been paying: 'It is plain that a life which includes deep resentment leads only to futility and unhappiness' (page 66). The book's way out is to see the people who wronged us as perhaps spiritually sick (page 66) and to ask God to help us show them the same tolerance, pity, and patience we would grant a sick friend (page 67), praying, 'God save me from being angry. Thy will be done' (page 67). Last comes the part many of us call the fourth column: 'Putting out of our minds the wrongs others had done, we resolutely looked for our own mistakes' (page 67). We ask, 'Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?' (page 67).

8161b45cd71b.t: Fear gets its own list because it touches nearly every part of our lives; the book describes it as an evil and corroding thread running through the fabric of our existence (page 67). The instruction is short: 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper, even though we had no resentment in connection with them' (page 68). For each fear we ask ourselves why we have it, and the book offers an honest answer: self-reliance failed us (page 68). The remedy is not grit but trust. 'We ask Him to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be' (page 68), and the book says we begin at once to outgrow fear.

bc9a3dd58e85.t: The third list reviews our own sex conduct over the years past (page 69). We ask where we were selfish, dishonest, or inconsiderate, whom we hurt, and whether we aroused jealousy, suspicion, or bitterness (page 69). We get it all down on paper and subject each relationship to one simple test: was it selfish or not (page 69)? From that honest look we shape a sane and sound ideal for our future sex life, and 'We asked God to mold our ideals and help us to live up to them' (page 69). If sex stays troublesome, page 70 gives a practical prescription: we throw ourselves harder into helping others, and we pray for the right ideal and for the strength to do the right thing.

679956cf5b7c.t: If we have been thorough, we have written down a lot (page 70). We have analyzed our resentments and listed the people we have hurt, becoming willing to straighten out the past (page 70). Then the book closes the inventory with reassurance instead of a grade: 'If you have already made a decision, and an inventory of your grosser handicaps, you have made a good beginning' (page 71). Step 4 does not have to be perfect. It has to be honest and on paper. The chapter ends by saying we have swallowed and digested some big chunks of truth about ourselves (page 71), and that truth is exactly what we carry with us into Step 5.

0bd744d4266e.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (Big Book), 4th Edition, Chapter 5 "How It Works": pages 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71

647378cae581.t: Where are the Step 4 instructions in the Big Book?

fe01128c6880.t: They run from the bottom of page 63 through page 71 in Chapter 5, How It Works. The resentment inventory is on pages 64 to 67, the fear inventory on pages 67 to 68, and the sex conduct review on pages 68 to 70, with page 71 calling a finished inventory a good beginning.

a1a8b0835677.t: Page 65 shows a sample list with three columns: who we are resentful at, the cause, and which part of self was affected, such as self-esteem, security, ambitions, or personal and sex relations. The direction many people call the fourth column comes on page 67, where we set aside the wrongs others did and look for our own mistakes, asking where we were selfish, dishonest, self-seeking, and frightened.

069076dbc40c.t: How do you do the fear inventory in the Big Book?

56423dbd0bd5.t: Page 68 says we reviewed our fears thoroughly and put them on paper even when no resentment was attached, then asked ourselves why we had them. The book's answer is that self-reliance failed us, so we ask God to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be (page 68).

4ebe737606e2.t: Does the Big Book say Step 4 has to be written down?

52e484db8948.t: Yes. The book says we set our resentments down on paper (page 64), put our fears on paper (page 68), and got the review of our sex conduct down on paper as well (page 69). Page 70 adds that if we have been thorough, we have written down a lot.

24001e9c8090.t: The Promises in the Big Book: Pages 83-84 Explained

e15b141830af.t: The Promises appear on pages 83-84 of the Big Book, just after the Ninth Step amends. Here is what they say and when the book says they materialize.

9a3172017009.t: <0>Home</0> / Big Book / The Promises: Big Book Pages 83-84

c61607c89224.t: What pages 83 and 84 promise us, and when the Big Book says those promises materialize

46b75d78f831.t: The Promises are found on pages 83 and 84 of <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, in the chapter called <1>Into Action</1>, immediately after the Big Book gives its directions for making Ninth Step amends. That placement is why members call them the Ninth Step Promises. They open with one of the most quoted lines in the whole book: 'We are going to know a new freedom and a new happiness' (page 83). From there the passage names, one by one, the changes that begin in an alcoholic who is cleaning up the wreckage of the past: freedom from regret, real serenity and peace, a past that becomes useful to others, the disappearance of self-pity and fear, and a whole new outlook on life.

d0bd2ebca391.t: When do they materialize? The book answers that plainly on page 84: 'They are being fulfilled among us—sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly. They will always materialize if we work for them.' So the Promises are not a graduation gift handed out after Step Twelve. Page 83 tells us we will be amazed before we are even half way through this phase of our development, which means the Promises start arriving while we are still in the middle of our amends. The only condition is the work itself.

1f68c0d73bf6.t: The passage reads like a portrait of a person being rebuilt. 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' (page 83). That single sentence turns our worst history into an asset, because the promise that follows says that however low we sank, our story can be used to help someone else (page 84). We will come to understand what serenity actually means, and we will know real peace (page 83). Feelings of uselessness and self-pity fade. We lose interest in selfish things and gain a genuine interest in the people around us, and self-seeking slips away (page 84). Our attitude toward life turns around completely, the fear of other people and of money trouble loses its grip, and we develop an instinct for handling the situations that once left us baffled (page 84). Then the passage closes with the heart of the entire program: 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' (page 84).

f0f196b1c5b4.t: The placement is not an accident. The paragraph that introduces the Promises says that when we are thorough and painstaking about this stage of our growth, the amazement comes before we are even half way through it (page 83), and the stage it means is making amends. The freedom the Promises describe is largely freedom from guilt, from dodging the people we have harmed, and from the fear of being found out, and that is exactly the debris Step Nine clears away. We cannot think our way into these results. The same page reminds us, 'The spiritual life is not a theory. We have to live it' (page 83). The Promises are simply what living it looks like.

d755a76c9dfc.t: Sometimes quickly, sometimes slowly. The book anticipates our skepticism and asks the question for us: 'Are these extravagant promises? We think not' (page 84). These lines were not written as a sales pitch but as a report of what the first members watched happen among themselves. Timelines differ. Some of us felt the fear lift within weeks, while others watched self-pity dissolve over years of steady work. The guarantee is conditional but absolute: always, if we work for them. And the Promises are not a finish line, because the very next lines on page 84 carry us straight into Step Ten. The maintenance steps keep producing the same results one day at a time, and page 85 reminds us that what we really have is a daily reprieve that depends on the condition of our spiritual life.

e2013a4d7502.t: Many groups read pages 83 and 84 aloud at meetings, and many of us keep them close as a plain-language description of where this road leads. They work best as a direction of travel, not a report card. If they feel far away today, the question the text puts to us is not whether we believe them yet but whether we are working for them. So we make the next amend, take the next inventory, and help the next alcoholic who reaches out. The Promises are still being fulfilled among us, at whatever pace our work sets, exactly as the book said they would be (page 84).

82b472c6bddc.t: — Alcoholics Anonymous (the Big Book), 4th Edition: pages 83-84 (the Ninth Step Promises, chapter 6, Into Action); page 83 (Ninth Step amends directions; the spiritual life is not a theory); page 84 (the Promises conclude; Step Ten follows immediately); page 85 (daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition).

054443d30d90.t: Where are the Promises in the Big Book?

9c2fd4563d17.t: The Promises are on pages 83 and 84 of Alcoholics Anonymous, 4th Edition, in the chapter called Into Action. They come immediately after the directions for making Ninth Step amends, which is why they are often called the Ninth Step Promises. Many groups read this passage aloud at meetings.

27138806f387.t: When do the Promises start to come true?

f80715d196cd.t: Sooner than most of us expect. Page 83 says we will be amazed before we are even half way through the amends process, so the Promises begin while we are still working Step Nine. Page 84 adds that they are fulfilled sometimes quickly and sometimes slowly, but always if we work for them.

29bb95c59ee9.t: Yes, with one condition. The Big Book says 'They will always materialize if we work for them' (page 84). The work is the program itself: making amends, taking daily inventory, prayer, and helping others, which are the very steps that surround the Promises in the text.

c9d269008d7b.t: How many promises are on pages 83-84?

175fd7291ea8.t: Most members count twelve promises in the passage, beginning with a new freedom and a new happiness and ending with the realization that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves (pages 83-84). The Big Book makes other promises throughout its chapters, but when someone refers to the Promises, they almost always mean these.
